text.en: Meena compared a picture of Athens with a timeline of Rome. She asked how a city-state’s assembly differed from an empire’s institutions.

This chapter studies the classical worlds of ancient Greece and Rome alongside empire-building in East Asia and the continuation of Roman rule in the east. Greece was made of city-states such as Athens and Sparta. Athens developed an early form of democracy in which citizens took part in the assembly.
Socrates, Plato and Aristotle helped shape traditions in Greek philosophy. Hippocrates is associated with an influential tradition of Greek medicine. Alexander the Great of Macedon built a vast empire that spread Greek culture.
Rome had kings before it became a republic. Much later Augustus established a form of imperial rule, even though some older institutions remained. The Romans built roads, aqueducts and the Colosseum and gave us Roman law and Latin. Imperial rule in the western Roman Empire ended in the fifth century CE. The eastern Roman Empire continued, with Constantinople as its capital.
This chapter studies the classical worlds of ancient Greece and Rome alongside empire-building in East Asia and the continuation of Roman rule in the east.
Greece was made of city-states such as Athens and Sparta.
Athens developed an early form of democracy in which citizens took part in the assembly.
Socrates, Plato and Aristotle helped shape traditions in Greek philosophy. Hippocrates is associated with an influential tradition of Greek medicine.
Alexander the Great of Macedon built a vast empire that spread Greek culture.
Rome had kings before it became a republic. Much later Augustus established a form of imperial rule, even though some older institutions remained.
The Romans built roads, aqueducts and the Colosseum and gave us Roman law and Latin.
Imperial rule in the western Roman Empire ended in the fifth century CE. The eastern Roman Empire continued, with Constantinople as its capital.
The Greek world included many poleis, or city-states. A polis could consist of an urban centre and nearby land. Geography and trade shaped the links between them.
Athens and Sparta had distinct institutions. Their inhabitants shared aspects of language and culture, but the two city-states did not have the same rules for political participation.

board.text: Shared culture can coexist with different institutions

text.en: In Athens, qualified citizens could deliberate and vote directly in the assembly. This is a historical example of direct participation.

board.text: Athenian assembly: citizen debate and voting

text.en: The Athenian citizen group excluded women, enslaved people and resident foreigners. Calling the system democratic should go together with asking who could take part.
Sparta organised much of its public life around military training and a narrow citizen body. Comparing it with Athens shows the variety of Greek city-state institutions.

board.text: Compare how the two poleis organised public life

text.en: The Persian Wars brought some Greek city-states into cooperation. Later conflict between Athens, Sparta and their allies shows that such cooperation did not create a single Greek state.

board.text: Cooperation and rivalry both shaped the Greek world

text.en: Greek drama, art and architecture survive in different forms. A theatre or a text can help explain how performance or public building was organised.

board.text: Material and literary evidence answer different questions

text.en: Alexander inherited power in Macedonia and conquered the Persian Empire. His campaigns connected many regions. After his death, successor kingdoms continued some of those connections.

board.text: Macedonian conquests gave way to successor kingdoms

text.en: Hellenistic culture developed where Greek traditions met those of Egypt, western Asia and other regions. Alexandria in Egypt was an important centre in this world.
The Roman Republic used institutions including assemblies, elected officials and a senate. The influence citizens could exercise depended on their status and on how those institutions worked.

board.text: Republic: several institutions shared political roles

text.en: Roman expansion brought new territories, trade and taxes. It also placed pressure on older institutions. Conquests and unequal access to resources contributed to internal tensions.
Augustus gained lasting authority after civil wars. The Senate still existed, but power increasingly centred on the emperor.

board.text: The imperial shift changed where power lay

text.en: Roads helped connect Roman towns and provinces. Aqueducts could carry water, often by gravity. Both show how infrastructure supported large settlements.

board.text: Roads connect places · aqueducts carry water

text.en: Roman law changed over centuries and influenced later legal traditions. Studying it does not require assuming that everyone in the empire had equal rights.

board.text: Influence of Roman law and unequal status coexist

text.en: In the eastern part of the chapter, the Qin unified several competing states in China. Standardising measures and written forms helped coordinate administration.
The Han dynasty followed and governed a large territory. Trade routes connected China with other areas through many communities. Exchange moved goods and ideas in stages.
Christianity began within the Roman world in the eastern Mediterranean. Communities and teachings spread across parts of the empire over time.
Under Constantine, Christians gained legal toleration in the empire. Later changes made Christianity more prominent in imperial public life. These developments took place over several decades.

board.text: Toleration and official prominence were separate changes

text.en: Constantinople occupied an important position between Europe and Asia. Its routes helped link the Black Sea and the Mediterranean world.
Western imperial rule ended in the fifth century. The Eastern Roman Empire continued from Constantinople and is often called the Byzantine Empire by modern historians.

board.text: Byzantine is a name for the Eastern Roman Empire

text.en: Political transitions do not always happen all at once. Buildings, laws, languages and religious communities can continue even when a form of rule changes.

board.text: Institutions can change at different rates

text.en: Compare a city-state with a large empire. Ask how each made decisions, linked its settlements and gathered resources. Use a specific example to support each comparison.

problem.en: Compare the Athenian assembly with authority under Augustus in the Roman Empire.

text.en: Ask who could take part in each setting.

why.en: Qualified Athenians could vote directly in the assembly. Many residents were excluded.

text.en: Ask who held growing authority under Augustus.

why.en: Power increasingly centred on the emperor even as older institutions remained.

prompt.en: A friend says The Roman Empire never fell. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: It fell in the 5th century CE.

points.en: Romans built roads and gave law.
